title: Contact Manifolds As A Toolkit
notes: Open by positioning the chapter as the first real toolkit chapter. Chapter 1 gave the contact condition; Chapter 2 asks what one can do with it: build examples, move structures by vector fields, normalize locally, and extend submanifold isotopies to ambient contactomorphisms.

title: The Chapter Thesis
notes: Frame the whole lecture around a single proof dependency. Moser-type equations produce vector fields; vector fields produce flows; flows produce equivalences and normal forms. Darboux, Gray stability, neighborhood theorems, and isotopy extension should feel like variations of one method, not isolated theorems.

title: First Examples: Same Contact Structure
notes: Use this slide to separate the form from the contact structure. A contactomorphism only has to carry the kernel distribution to the other kernel, so the pullback may be multiplied by a nowhere-zero function. The explicit standard-to-polar calculation is a quick sanity check that formulas are not decorative.

title: Standard Versus Overtwisted R3
notes: The overtwisted example should be drawn as changing contact planes along a radial ray, not as a copied textbook figure. The point is that the local nonintegrability condition can hold while the plane field contains a disk-level witness for flexibility that standard contact space does not.

title: Gray Stability: Follow The Planes
notes: Explain Gray stability as the global version of moving along the family rather than freezing one form. On a closed manifold, a smooth family of contact structures is tracked by an isotopy whose differential carries the initial plane field to the current one.

title: Strict Contact Forms Fail To Stay Fixed
notes: This is the cautionary slide. Gray stability concerns contact structures, not strict equality of contact forms. On S three, changing a contact form can change Reeb orbit behavior, such as rational versus irrational closures on tori, and strict contactomorphisms would preserve that behavior.

title: Contact Hamiltonians Encode Vector Fields
notes: Put the two equations in the center and dwell on their asymmetry. The first equation fixes the Reeb component of the vector field. The second equation then chooses the horizontal part so the contact condition is preserved up to conformal scaling.

title: Three Hamiltonians In The Standard Model
notes: Read the table as a finite lab. The constant Hamiltonian is pure Reeb motion, the linear Hamiltonian produces a horizontal tilt, and the quadratic Hamiltonian forces planar rotation plus a vertical correction. The JSON file gives a compact reproducible check of these coefficients.

title: The Quadratic Flow Check
notes: Use the local artifact as evidence, not as a substitute for the theorem. The streamlines show rotation in the x y plane, while the color records the z correction. The residuals verify that alpha of X equals H and that the contraction equation has zero symbolic error.

title: Symplectic Vector Bundles
notes: This interlude supplies the language used by neighborhood theorems. Once each contact plane is a symplectic vector space, compatible complex structures and almost contact structures become flexible choices rather than extra rigid data. Contractibility is the reason the choices do not introduce new local invariants.

title: Darboux: No Local Invariants
notes: Present Darboux as the local endpoint of Moser thinking. Around a point, every contact form can be changed by coordinates into the standard model. The anisotropic scaling explains why contact geometry treats the z direction as quadratic relative to x and y.

title: Isotropic Neighborhood Data
notes: For isotropic submanifolds, the important invariant is not the whole ambient manifold but the conformal symplectic normal data. The splitting shows what gets remembered: the Reeb line, the J image of tangent directions, and the conformal symplectic normal quotient.

title: Legendrian Neighborhood Model
notes: Legendrian neighborhoods are the cleanest case because TL is Lagrangian in xi along L, so the conformal symplectic normal part disappears. The first jet space model uses the source convention alpha equals dz minus the canonical one-form; it should sound familiar from front projections: base position, covector slope, and height form the universal local contact chart.

title: Contact Submanifold Neighborhoods
notes: A contact submanifold has its own contact planes, so the normal data is symplectic inside the ambient contact distribution. The theorem's invariant input is the contactomorphism on the submanifold together with a CSNM isomorphism; Reeb direction alignment belongs to the proof's local-model normalization after forms are chosen.

title: Characteristic Foliations On Hypersurfaces
notes: This slide shifts from submanifolds that inherit contact data to hypersurfaces that record a line field. In dimension three the characteristic foliation is especially visible: tangent directions are those that lie in both the surface tangent plane and the contact plane.

title: Isotopy Extension By Hamiltonians
notes: Now turn the direction of reasoning around. Given an isotopy of a special submanifold, define a Hamiltonian along it, extend that function with a bump, and integrate the corresponding contact Hamiltonian vector field. The bump is what keeps the construction local.

title: Contact Disc Theorem And Alexander Trick
notes: Describe the contact disc theorem as a final local flexibility statement. Shrinking a contact embedding by the anisotropic contact dilations gives the contact linearization S0j, not merely the ordinary derivative. Its conformal symplectic linear part is controlled by the connectedness of the positive conformal symplectic group, which removes the remaining linear obstruction.

title: One Toolkit
notes: Close by returning to the chapter thesis. Preserve, normalize, and extend are not separate instincts: each one solves a vector-field equation and checks what data must remain fixed. The artifacts record the Hamiltonian version of the same proof habit.
